Rule 91's operational test points the other way — `ἡλίκος` occurs nowhere in the corpus but inside this verse, and the neighbouring classes are unanimous: the sibling correlative `πηλίκος` → *how large* heads on *large* (GAL.6.11), `ὅσα` → *how much soever* on *much* (REV.18.7) and `ὅσαι` → *how many soever be* on *many* (2CO.1.20), and the `how …` frame heads its content word throughout. Expressed conjunction → and.

Head on *fire*, the meaning-bearing complement carrying the `φλογ-` lexeme's sense, as rule 17 heads *make straight* on *straight* and rule 91 heads *make known* on *known*; a head on *setteth* would rest only on its being the finite word, which rule 17 refuses. `φλογίζω` occurs nowhere in the corpus outside this verse and `πυρόω` nowhere at all, so rule 91's lemma query returns nothing and the frame query decides instead: where one source verb is rendered by English *set* plus a complement the corpus heads the complement without exception — `ἠλευθέρωσεν` → *did set free* on *free* (GAL.5.1), `ἐσφράγισεν` → *hath set his seal* on *seal* (JHN.3.33), `ἀθετοῦσιν` → *set at nought* on *nought* (JUD.1.8), `ἐλπίσατε` → *and set your hope* on *hope* (1PE.1.13, JHN.5.45), and `πυρούμενοι` → *being on fire* on *fire* (2PE.3.12). The units that do head on *set* are rule 91's contrast working correctly, their lexemes meaning set or establish. JAS.3.10's `ἐξέρχεται` → *cometh forth* headed on *cometh* is consistent rather than in tension: `ἔρχομαι` means *come*, so there the verb word glosses the lexeme.
Article realized as the (rule 19).
τροχόν → wheel.
The ASV gives nature no determiner, so this article has no the to anchor (rule 23).
Genitive noun rendered of + nature; the case preposition rides with the noun under rule 21's determinerless clause, headed on the noun.
Expressed conjunction → and. The bracketed itself of the gloss has no ASV realization and is not aligned.

Passive participle → *is set on fire*; the auxiliary rides inside the unit under rule 9. Head on *fire*, matching the active `φλογίζουσα` above (rule 24) and the corpus's *set* + complement frame cited there.
Agentive ὑπό → by (rule 36).
Article before γεέννης, which the ASV renders by a bare hell with no determiner supplied (rule 23).
γεέννης → hell (the greek_gloss note records Gehenna and changes no correspondence).

review_notes: Corrected s016/s017. The accepted alignment read ἡ σπιλοῦσα as a substantival article under rule 90, giving which to the article and defileth to the participle. Rule 90 disclaims that in terms — it blesses no unit in which a head noun is expressed — and one is expressed here: γλῶσσα (s010) stands in the same clause, agrees with the article in gender, number and case, and is the antecedent the ASV's which relativizes. The construction is rule 31's second attributive article, so the article is unrepresented and which is a helper on the participle, headed on defileth.

The verse's own alternative_rendering notes are the decisive evidence for that change: both spell the substantival construal out as 'that which', which is what the ASV would have written had it read ἡ σπιλοῦσα as rule 90's shape. Its main text writes a plain relative on an expressed antecedent instead, which is rule 31's τῷ θεῷ τῷ κτίσαντι → God who created.

The discontinuity between γλῶσσα and its trailing article (καθίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν intervening) does not defeat the expressed-head-noun test: rule 15 permits a discontinuous unit and rule 57 has an attributive article governing its head noun across whatever stands between them.

Clause division follows the ASV's punctuation and is unchanged: the tongue is a fire is one verbless clause with rule 63 putting the supplied is on the predicate nominal fire, and καθίσταται supplies the second clause's own expressed verb, so no second copula is supplied anywhere.

Both φλογίζω units head on fire rather than on the finite verb word, under rule 17's meaning-bearing-complement clause, keeping the active and passive analyses identical under rule 24. The lexeme is unattested elsewhere in the corpus, so rule 91's query returns nothing and the head rests on the make straight / make known analogy; a later reader with corpus evidence for φλογίζω should check it.

Every article is decided separately (rule 13): s002, s005, s009, s019, s023 take the ASV's the; s007, s025, s030 are unrepresented for want of a determiner; s013 is emptied by the free genitive ἡμῶν under rule 20; s016 is now unrepresented under rule 31. No article in this verse is aligned to a relativizer.
A reference comparison will report s016 as an unrepresented article and therefore as a disagreement with the rule 90 reading; the note on that unit names the competing analysis.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV renders no resumptive "so" or "thus" after "the world of iniquity": "the world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defileth...". None of the three alternative_rendering notes supplies οὕτως either, so the RP addition is unrepresented.

alignments.note: Postpositive γάρ realized by the verse-opening For.
Universal πᾶσα → every; no article or negator stands with it, so rules 80 and 87 are not in question.
φύσις → kind, the ASV's gloss here (marginal note: Greek nature).

Genitive noun rendered of + noun; rule 17 heads on the noun and rule 21's case preposition rides along, no article standing. The of governs the coordinated πετεινῶν as well and stays on the first genitive under rule 2.

Correlative τε of the τε … καί pair: the ASV writes a single and for the pair and no both, so nothing answers to the particle (rule 23; rule 65's English-side test for a correlative particle, as rule 70 applies it to μέν). Giving the and to τε and emptying καί is the mirror reading; the corpus puts the written word on the ordinary conjunction. The corpus decides a `τε … καί` pair the same way and cites no other: 2CO.12.12 empties `τε` because the following `καί` already takes the one written *and*, and REV.19.18 does both within one verse, emptying the `τε` that has no English while giving *both* to the one that does. The mirror reading has no corpus unit. Note the corpus lemma is the accented `τέ`; a query on `τε` returns nothing and is a false negative.
καί → and, the one conjunction word the ASV writes for τε … καί.
πετεινῶν → birds; the ASV gives this genitive no of of its own, the earlier of at t004 governing both, so the noun stands alone.

One Greek noun rendered by modifier + noun, headed on *creeping*. Rule 66 asks whether the English noun glosses the lexeme or is a supplied generic completion, and rule 91 makes that test operational: the corpus never spends a bare *things* on this word, and where it renders a single creeping-thing substantive by this very English phrase it heads the modifier every time — `רֶמֶשׂ` → *creeping things* at 1KI.4.33, GEN.1.24 and GEN.6.7 and → *creeping thing* at GEN.1.26 and GEN.6.20, five units to none, 1KI.4.33 saying in terms that *creeping* carries the lexeme and *things* is the generic noun supplied. Corrected from a head on *things*, which rested on an analogy to `ζῷον` → *living creature* and `κτίσμα` → *created thing*; that analogy fails rule 91's own test, because the corpus spends bare *creature(s)* and *thing* on those lexemes and so their English noun is a real gloss, whereas *things* here is not. `ἑρπετόν` occurs nowhere in the corpus outside this verse and `ἕρπω` nowhere at all, so no lemma query is available and the phrase query is what decides. This also brings the unit into step with the same chapter's `μεγάλα` → *great things* headed on *great* at JAS.3.5 (rule 24). The case preposition *of* rides with the noun under rule 21, no article standing, and it governs the coordinated `ἐναλίων` as well.
Second correlative τε, empty for the same reason as s005: the ASV writes only and for the pair. Same precedent as s005: 2CO.12.12 and REV.19.18.
καί → and.

Anarthrous substantival adjective: no Greek article competes, so the supplied *things* and its determiner are rule 7 helpers on the adjective (rules 51, 58, 102). Rule 17's generic-noun clause keeps the head on *sea*, the word realizing the `ἐνάλιος` lexeme, rather than on the completion *things*. `ἐνάλιος` occurs nowhere in the corpus, in either testament, so the reading rests on the rule text and on the nearest shape precedent, `ἄραφος` → *without seam* headed on *seam* at JHN.19.23. The source's part of speech is not what decides this: rule 66 extends rule 17's test to a noun rather than opposing it, which is why s008 now heads on *creeping* on the same reasoning.
Present passive with its auxiliary; rule 9 heads on the lexical verb tamed.
Expressed καί joining the two verbs → and.
Perfect passive with its auxiliaries; rule 9 heads on tamed.
The ASV gives the dative phrase no determiner, so the article has no the to anchor and the case preposition stays with the noun (rules 21, 23).

The ASV compresses `φύσει ἀνθρωπίνῃ` into the single word *mankind*, whose parts answer to both lexemes — *kind* to `φύσις` (as at t003) and *man-* to `ἀνθρωπίνῃ` — so rule 39's test keeps the pair one `aligned` unit rather than `noncompositional`; rule 21 gives the case preposition *by* to this unit, no article being available to carry it, as rule 21's own worked `τῇ προσευχῇ` → *by prayer* does at PHP.4.6. The corpus builds such a unit elsewhere and not only for prepositions: `πάντας αἰῶνας` → *evermore* at JUD.1.25 is the same adjective-plus-noun shape headed on the noun, and `ληνὸν οἴνου` → *winepress* at REV.19.15 the same parts-answer test. Source head on the noun `φύσει` under rule 10's syntactic head and target head on *mankind* under rule 17; REV.9.20 spends the whole of *mankind* on `ἀνθρώπων`, which is why rule 10's syntactic head rather than a lexical one settles it, 1PE.2.13 spending only *man* on `ἀνθρώπινος` and EPH.2.3, GAL.2.15 and GAL.4.8 spending *nature* on `φύσις`. Splitting — `φύσει` taking *by mankind* and `ἀνθρωπίνῃ` left `unrepresented` — remains defensible, as REV.19.15 and 2PE.3.18 concede for their own second tokens; what is unavailable is sharing *mankind* between two units, the ledger forbidding a target token in more than one.
Second attributive article of τῇ φύσει τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, which English realizes nowhere (rule 23).

review_notes: One change from the accepted alignment: s008 ἑρπετῶν → of creeping things now heads on t010 things rather than t009 creeping. The accepted note distinguished ἑρπετόν from κτίσμα by decomposing the Greek — "that noun's own lexeme is thing-created whereas ἑρπετόν's is the creeping" — but that distinction does not survive inspection, since κτίσμα's sense-bearing element is equally the creating and rule 66 still heads it on thing. Rules 91 and 99 replace the compositional argument with what the corpus spends on the lexeme, and the two nearest listed precedents in both English shape and Greek formation, ζῷον → living creature and κτίσμα → created thing, both head on the entity noun.

That change rests on analogy alone: neither ἑρπετόν nor any ἑρπ- word occurs elsewhere in the finalized corpus, so rule 91's lemma query has nothing to return. A head on creeping on the analogy of πλεονέκτης → covetous man remains defensible and a later reader with a wider corpus should re-run the query before treating this as settled.

s008 and s011 now head differently — things versus sea — and that is deliberate, not an inconsistency. s008 is N-GPN and falls under rule 66; s011 is A-GPN, a substantival adjective whose own English word is in the sea, so rule 17's generic-noun clause keeps the head off the supplied things.

Everything else stands as accepted. Both τε particles are unrepresented because the ASV writes a single and for each τε … καί pair; giving the and to τε and emptying καί is the mirror reading, but rules 65 and 70's English-side test puts the written word on the ordinary conjunction. A reference comparison will report both as disagreements.

s016 + s018 form the verse's only many-to-one unit, forced by the ASV's portmanteau mankind: one English token cannot be partitioned. It stays aligned rather than noncompositional because -kind answers to φύσις and man- to ἀνθρωπίνῃ under rule 39's test, and it carries the case preposition by because the ASV supplies no determiner for either article to anchor (rules 21, 23).

alignments.note: Postpositive δέ realized by the verse-initial *but*.
Article surfaces as *the* under rule 19; split from its noun under rule 26.
Noun stands alone, its determiner having gone to the article.

δύναται is itself the modal lexeme, so *can* is its own word and not an auxiliary borrowed from the infinitive; the infinitive keeps *tame*. Rule 39's `οὐ δύναται` → *cannot* is not in question, the ASV writing the negation as a separate *no*.
οὐδείς takes *no*. Rules 41 and 59 are not in question: no separate negator stands in the clause for the indefinite to empty.

Partitive genitive ἀνθρώπων rendered by the singular *man* of *no man*. Rule 2 splits it from οὐδείς, both pieces remaining independently recoverable; the competing reading takes *no man* as one unit on οὐδείς with ἀνθρώπων unrepresented, but the ASV's *man* answers to this lexeme and nothing else. Rule 69's `οὐδένα` → *any man* is not the model, the *man* there being a supplied completion with no source token behind it.
Infinitive complement rendered by the bare *tame*, the modal riding with δύναται.

Verbless clause with no expressed subject, so under rule 68 the predicate carries both the supplied subject *it* and the copula *is*; κακόν is the substantival adjective serving as the nominal word of the predicate phrase, so under rule 58's substantival clause it also takes the supplied determiner *a*, ἀκατάστατον being only an attributive modifier inside the phrase. Discontinuous under rule 15.
Attributive adjective inside the predicate noun phrase keeps a bare *restless*; the determiner belongs to the nominal word under rule 58, not to the adjective it stands next to.
Second verbless clause, again with no expressed subject: the adjectival predicate takes the supplied *it is* along with its own *full* under rules 53 and 68.

Genitive complement rendered *of poison*; the ASV supplies no determiner, so under rule 21's determinerless clause the case preposition stays with the noun. Discontinuous around *deadly* under rule 15.
Attributive adjective takes the bare *deadly*, split from its noun under rule 26.

review_notes: Reviewed unchanged. All 12 source and all 18 target ids partition exactly once; every unit is `aligned` with nonempty arrays and heads inside them, so rules 1, 3 and 10 hold.

Both verbless clauses lack an expressed subject, so rule 68 puts the supplied *it is* on the predicate rather than on any subject token; rules 53 and 63 do not reach them, there being no subject pronoun and no subject noun.

The *a* of *a restless evil* was re-checked. κακόν is a substantival A-NSN doing the nominal work, ἀκατάστατον only attributive, so the determiner is the nominal word's under rule 58 either way — by its main clause if κακόν is read as the phrase's noun, by its substantival clause (`νεκρῶν` → *the dead*) if it is read as an adjective. Rule 102 is not in question, the Greek being anarthrous with no article to take the determiner.
The one materially contested unit is the *no man* split across οὐδείς and ἀνθρώπων; the competing whole-phrase reading on οὐδείς with ἀνθρώπων unrepresented is named in the s007 note.

Both variant units are informational only: v008 (s005–s007) is underdetermined with the base among the compatible readings, and v009 (s008) is a selected base. Neither is marked FALLBACK EXCLUDED BY EVIDENCE, so rule 97 is not engaged and no token needs `added`.

variant_decisions.evidence: The variation is the order of δαμάσαι, δύναται and ἀνθρώπων only; ASV's "the tongue can no man tame" is a fixed English ordering that reflects either arrangement.
ASV "a restless evil" renders ἀκατάστατον (unsettled, restless); ἀκατάσχετον means uncontrollable/unruly and would have given "an unruly evil" as in the earlier English tradition.

alignments.note: Rule 81: preposition fused with its governed pronoun into a single English *there-* word; *there-* answers to the pronoun and *-with* to `ἐν`, so the pair is one `aligned` unit headed on the pronominal, not `noncompositional` under rule 45. Rule 81's own examples `ἐν αὐτῷ` → *therein* and `δι᾽ αὐτῆς` → *thereby* are pronominals, so the rule reaches a personal pronoun and not only a demonstrative.
Rule 9: the inflected verb takes its English subject pronoun; the lexical verb is the head. The ASV's inversion *bless we* is English word order and does not move the head (rule 17).
Rule 19: the article surfaces as *the*. The packet gloss *our* is not what the ASV wrote, and no English possessive stands here to displace it under rule 20 or to be recovered under rule 76.
Rule 26: the noun is independently recoverable and is split from its article.
Coordinating conjunction realized by *and*.
The second coordinated noun stands bare; the single article governs the whole phrase and has already taken *the*.
Clause-coordinating conjunction realized by *and*.
Rule 81 again, as with s001–s002; the ASV repeats the portmanteau and the analysis is the same one (rule 24).
Rule 9: subject pronoun rides with the verb, headed on the lexical verb *curse*.
Rule 23: the ASV gives *men* no determiner, so the article has no English realization. Rule 13 forbids grouping it with its noun for convenience.
Bare *men*, its article `unrepresented` above.

Rule 31: the article follows an expressed head noun (`ἀνθρώπους`) and a participle follows it, so the participle carries the supplied relativizer and copula and the second attributive article is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 23. The competing reading would give *who* to the article under rule 32 or rule 90, but both are scoped to a substantival article governing no head noun, which is not the case here. Rule 31's prepositional-phrase carve-out does not reach this either: `καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν θεοῦ` sits inside the participial phrase, and the participle is the verb that carries the relativizer.
Rule 36: the English preposition governing the phrase realizes the Greek preposition.

Rule 51's anarthrous clause: no Greek article stands here, so the supplied *the* is an ordinary rule 7 helper on the noun it determines, and the noun is the head. Rule 21 has no article to anchor the determiner, so *the* does not ride with `καθ᾽`.
Rule 17: for a source noun rendered by *of + noun*, the noun is the head; the *of* realizes the genitive and rides with it, no article standing to anchor it (rule 21).

Rule 31: the attributive participle is recast as a finite relative clause, so the relativizer *who* and the copula *are* are its helpers under rules 7 and 9, headed on the lexical participle *made* rather than on the copula (rule 17). Rule 15 permits the unit's distance from `καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν θεοῦ`, which keeps its own English words.

review_notes: Reviewed unchanged: every unit of the accepted alignment survives review. The partition is complete — all 18 source and all 20 target ids appear exactly once.

Both `ἐν αὐτῇ` phrases go to rule 81 (`aligned`, headed on the pronoun) rather than rule 45 `noncompositional`, since *-with* answers to the preposition and *there-* to the pronoun. Rule 81's cited units include `ἐν αὐτῷ` → *therein* and `δι᾽ αὐτῆς` → *thereby*, both governing personal pronouns, so the rule is not confined to demonstratives.
s004 takes *the* despite the packet gloss *our*: no English possessive is written, so rules 20 and 76 do not arise.
s012 and s014 are both `unrepresented` for different reasons — no determiner written for *men* (rule 23), and an article after an expressed head noun with a participle following (rule 31).

A reference comparison may report s014 as represented if it reads *who* off the article; rule 31's expressed-head-noun test is what decides against that, and rule 90 says in terms that it blesses no unit in which a head noun is expressed.

s016's supplied *the* stays on `ὁμοίωσιν` and does not ride with `καθ᾽`: the Greek is anarthrous, so rule 51's anarthrous clause makes the determiner a rule 7 helper on the word it determines, and rule 21 has no article here to carry a case preposition.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV "bless we the Lord and Father" renders κύριον; θεόν would have produced "God the Father" — and ASV does write "God" later in the same verse for θεοῦ, showing it distinguishes the two words.

alignments.note: Expressed Greek preposition takes the whole English preposition 'out of' (rule 36); the article behind it keeps a bare 'the' under rule 19, since rule 21's case preposition is owed to an article only where no Greek preposition is expressed to hold it. Giving 'of' to the article was rejected on that ground.
Article realized by 'the' (rule 19). The intensive 'same' does not displace it: the ASV writes both words, so rule 38's displacement does not apply and the determiner slot is the article's own.
Attributive intensive αὐτοῦ → 'same', split from the article under rule 26. This is the identity adjective, not a demonstrative, so rule 38 is not in question.
Head noun, bare behind its own article (rule 57).

Finite verb with its English particle; 'forth' is part of the phrasal rendering of ἐξέρχομαι and answers to no separate source token — s001 ἐκ already has its own 'out of'. Head on the verb word 'cometh' under rule 91's operational test, the corpus spending the verb word on ἔρχομαι-compounds.
Subject noun.
Expressed conjunction.
Second subject noun.

Ordinary negative aligned to 'not'; discontinuity permitted by rule 15, the ASV placing it after 'ought'. No negative indefinite stands here, so rules 41 and 59 are not in question, and the ASV writes two words rather than one, so rule 39 does not join it to χρή.
Impersonal χρή → 'ought'.
Anarthrous vocative; no article stands, so rule 89 is not in question and the noun takes 'brethren' alone. The ASV supplies no address word here — 'My' answers to μου.
Genitive pronoun carries the possessive 'My'.

Substantival demonstrative with no article in question (rule 38's closing clause); the generic 'things' expands it and rule 17's generic-noun clause keeps the head on the demonstrative, as rule 99 cites for ταῦτα → 'these things'.
Adverb → 'so'. No καί answers it here and the ASV writes no correlative 'even so', so rules 82 and 100 are not in question.
No preposition governs the infinitive, so the infinitival 'to' is a rule 7 helper on its verb (rule 61); head on the lexical verb 'be'.

review_notes: Reviewed unchanged. All 15 source and 19 target ids partitioned exactly once; no unrepresented or added units in this verse.

s001/s002: 'out of' stays whole on the expressed preposition ἐκ. Rule 21 hands a case preposition to the article only where no Greek preposition is expressed to carry it (rule 36), and rule 95's REV.14.10 shape says in terms that an article standing after such a rendering is not owed an 'of the'. The competing reading — 'out' to ἐκ and 'of the' to the article — was rejected on that ground.

s002/s003: 'the same' is split because the ASV writes a determiner and the intensive separately; αὐτοῦ here is the identity adjective in attributive position, not a demonstrative, and rule 38 empties an article only where another source word occupies the English determiner slot, which is not the case when the ASV writes 'the' itself.

s009: 'not' is discontinuous from its clause-initial Greek position; the alternative of folding it with χρή into a single unit was rejected because the ASV writes two independent English words (rules 2 and 39), and rule 15 already permits the discontinuity.

s005 head: 'cometh' rather than 'forth'. 'forth' is the particle of the phrasal rendering of the compound verb and answers to no separate source token, s001 ἐκ having its own 'out of'; rule 91's operational test puts the head on the word the corpus spends on the lexeme, which for ἔρχομαι-compounds is the verb word.

alignments.note: Interrogative μήτι expecting a negative answer. The ASV marks the question by inversion alone; the supplied *Doth* is the do-support auxiliary English inversion requires, carrying only the tense and agreement of βρύει, so it rides with the finite verb under rule 9, exactly as `μὴ πλείονα σημεῖα ποιήσει;` → *will he do more signs?* in rule 44. The competing reading takes *Doth* as a supplied interrogative word under rule 64 (`μήτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστός;` → *Can this be the Christ?*); rejected because *Can* there is a modal the Greek never wrote, whereas *doth send* is only the periphrastic form of βρύει — rule 64's own carve-out for a word the clause would have required anyway. A reference comparison will report this token as a disagreement; rules 44 and 64 say that report is not a correction.
Article before its expressed noun, realized as *the* under rule 19.
πηγή → *fountain*, split from its article under rule 26.
ἐκ → *from*; the English preposition governing the phrase realizes the Greek preposition under rule 36, not the phrasal verb *send forth*, whose *forth* is its own particle.
Article takes the English determiner *the*; the case preposition is already realized by the expressed ἐκ, so rule 21's *of the* pattern does not arise and the article stands alone on *the*.

Identity adjective αὐτῆς → *same*. It does not empty the article: rule 20's displacement is for a possessive and rule 38's for a demonstrative, and αὐτός in attributive position is neither — *the same opening* keeps the article's own *the* under rule 19.
ὀπῆς → *opening*, recoverable independently of its article under rule 26.

βρύει → *Doth send forth*, discontinuous under rule 15 because the interrogative inversion fronts the auxiliary. Rules 9 and 17 head the unit on the lexical verb *send* rather than the auxiliary *Doth*; *forth* is the English verb's own particle, not a realization of ἐκ (rule 36).

Article governing the substantival adjective γλυκύ. Rules 49 and 102 give the article the nominal the ASV supplies for it — here *water*, italicized in the ASV, which rule 11 makes evidence rather than a verdict — leaving the adjective bare. No determiner is written, so the article takes the supplied noun only, headed on it (rule 102: all corpus units of this shape head on the nominal, never on a determiner). Rule 17's generic-noun clause is not the contrast, being scoped to anarthrous Greek where no article stands to take the supplied word.
γλυκύ → *sweet*, bare, its supplied nominal having gone to the article beside it under rule 102.
Coordinating καί → *and*.

Second substantival article. The ASV supplies no second nominal and no determiner for *bitter* — the elided *water* is not rewritten — so nothing is left for the article to realize and rule 23 makes it its own unit. This is not rule 102's case, which needs an English word the article can take; the asymmetry with s009 is the ASV's own.
πικρόν → *bitter*, the substantival adjective standing alone.

review_notes: Reviewed and returned unchanged in substance; two notes were expanded (s001, s006, s009) to name the competing reading and the rule that excludes it, per rule 16. No unit's ids, status or heads were altered.
Partition checked: s001–s013 and t001–t013 each appear exactly once. s008 is the only multi-target unit (t001, t004, t005), discontinuous under rule 15.

s001 is the one genuinely contested unit. The question is whether *Doth* is a supplied interrogative word (rule 64, → aligned) or the do-support auxiliary English inversion requires of a lexical verb (rules 9 and 44, → unrepresented). Held to unrepresented: *Doth* carries nothing but βρύει's tense and agreement, the lexical verb standing nonfinite beside it, whereas rule 64's *Can* and *Can it be that* add modal or framing content the Greek never wrote. Rule 64's own carve-out — a copula the clause would have required anyway is not a supplied word — is the same reasoning. A reference comparison will report this token as a disagreement and that is not a correction.

s009/s012 asymmetry checked against rules 49 and 102: the first article takes the supplied *water* because a substantival adjective leaves nothing else to carry it, and the second is unrepresented because the ASV elides rather than repeats the noun. Rule 102's corpus is unanimous on heading such a unit on the nominal, so t011 is the head and not any determiner (none is written here in any case).

s006 checked for article-emptying: αὐτός in attributive position is an identity adjective, not a possessive (rule 20) or a demonstrative (rules 38, 49), so *the same opening* leaves the article its own *the* under rule 19 and αὐτῆς takes only *same*.
Heads reviewed separately from edges per rule 28: s008 on *send* rather than the fronted auxiliary, s004 on *from* rather than the verb's *forth* particle (rule 36), s009 on the supplied nominal.

alignments.note: Interrogative μή expecting a negative answer. The ASV marks the question by inversion alone ("can a fig tree ... yield olives") and supplies no interrogative word, so under rule 44 the particle is its own unrepresented unit. A reference comparison will report this as a disagreement; that report is not a correction.
δύναται is the expressed modal and takes the first *can*.

Anarthrous vocative; no article competes, so the noun stands on its own English word (rule 89's anarthrous clause). No supplied address word (*ye*, *O*) is written here, so nothing further rides along.
Genitive pronoun carries the possessive *my*; no article is present to be displaced (rule 20).
